nodes.title: Plasma cell deficiency in human subjects with heterozygous mutations in Sec61 translocon alpha 1 subunit (SEC61A1).

nodes.label: Taubenheim et al. (2012)
nodes.title: High rate of antibody secretion is not integral to plasma cell differentiation as revealed by XBP-1 deficiency.

nodes.label: Reimold et al. (2001)
nodes.title: Plasma cell differentiation requires the transcription factor XBP-1.

nodes.label: Reimold et al. (2001) found that mouse lymphoid chimeras lacking XBP-1 had normal numbers of activated B lymphocytes, which proliferated, secreted cytokines and formed normal germinal centers. However, the chimeras secreted very little immunoglobulin of any isotype and could not control infection with the B-cell-dependent polyoma virus, because plasma cells were markedly absent.

Reimold et al. (2001) found that XBP-1 transcripts rose rapidly in vitro after stimuli that induce plasma cell differentiation and were present at high levels in plasma cells from rheumatoid synovium. Introducing XBP-1 into B-lineage cells started plasma cell differentiation. The authors concluded that XBP-1 is the only transcription factor known to be selectively and specifically required for terminal differentiation of B lymphocytes into plasma cells.

Taubenheim et al. (2012) studied XBP-1-deficient mouse B cells in vitro and in vivo. Antibody-secreting cells (ASCs) were still generated efficiently without XBP-1. In resting and immunized mice, ASCs were present at normal frequencies and showed the surface markers typical of plasma cells. Antibody secretion was reduced but not abolished, and the cells did not develop the morphology characteristic of ASCs. The authors concluded that plasma cell differentiation can proceed relatively normally without high rates of immunoglobulin secretion.

Schubert et al. (2018) studied 10 individuals in a family (Family I) with antibody isotype deficiencies involving IgM, IgG and IgA and severe recurrent bacterial infections, including tonsillitis, otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia and gastrointestinal infections. Onset was mostly in the first year of life. Affected individuals did not respond to polysaccharide vaccination and responded variably to tetanus toxoid vaccination. Infections became markedly fewer and less severe after IVIG replacement therapy was started.
Recurrent infection of the gastrointestinal tract
Decreased specific antibody response to unconjugated polysaccharide vaccine

Schubert et al. (2018) described Family II, in which the index patient (II.P3) was an 8-year-old boy with hypogammaglobulinemia since birth. With IVIG treatment he had no severe or recurrent infections, but repeated attempts to withdraw IVIG failed because his Ig levels stayed low. His grandmother, a mutation carrier, had more frequent upper respiratory infections and recurrent bilateral bacterial otitis media in childhood. At age 66 years her serum immunoglobulin levels were normal.

Schubert et al. (2018) found normal B-, T- and NK-cell ratios in patients from both families. T-cell subsets, regulatory T cells and recent thymic emigrants were normal. Peripheral B-cell subpopulations were also normal, including naive, unswitched memory, switched memory, transitional and CD21-low B cells. Only the very small CD27+CD38-high plasmablast population appeared reduced in Family I.

Schubert et al. (2018) performed a genome-wide linkage analysis with microsatellite markers in Family I and found linkage to chromosome 3 between markers D3S3697 and D3S3684. The peak LOD score was 3.31.

Schubert et al. (2018) performed whole-exome sequencing on 4 affected and 2 unaffected members of Family I and identified a heterozygous c.254T>A transversion in SEC61A1, predicting a Val85Asp (V85D) substitution. SEC61A1 was the only candidate gene in the chromosome 3 linkage region, and Sanger sequencing confirmed that the variant segregated perfectly with the disease. V85 is highly conserved and is one of the 6 pore-ring residues of the Sec61 channel. In HeLa cells, the V85D mutant had impaired cotranslational translocation of preprolactin, and its overexpression lowered the ER calcium load, which the authors concluded was a dominant effect.

Schubert et al. (2018) carried out targeted next-generation sequencing in more than 200 additional patients with primary antibody deficiency and found a heterozygous c.1325G>T nonsense variant in SEC61A1 (p.E381*) in the index patient of Family II. His grandmother and mother also carried the variant. gnomAD contained no premature stop codons in SEC61A1. SEC61A1 protein was reduced in the patients' naive B cells, and no truncated protein was detected. The authors suggested that the variant causes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and haploinsufficiency, with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.

Schubert et al. (2018) found that B cells from mutation carriers in both families made significantly fewer plasmablasts and plasma cells after in vitro stimulation, both T cell-dependent and T cell-independent, and produced less IgG and IgA. EBV-transformed B-cell lines from patients had less SEC61A1, lacked a CD38-high/CD138+ plasma cell subpopulation, and secreted less immunoglobulin.

Schubert et al. (2018) found that SEC61A1-V85D overexpression depleted the ER calcium store in HeLa cells, suggesting increased Ca2+ leakage. In multiple myeloma cell lines, stable expression of the mutant led to loss of the transduced cells and activated the terminal UPR, with upregulation of IRE1A, PERK, XBP1s, ATF4 and CHOP. Other cell lines were not affected. In thapsigargin-treated HEK293T cells, the V85D mutant had a dominant effect on XBP1s induction. The authors concluded that the mutation selectively impairs plasma cell survival.

Schubert et al. (2018) suggested that SEC61A1 haploinsufficiency causes possibly transient hypogammaglobulinemia with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance in Family II. In contrast, they proposed that the dominant-negative V85D missense mutation is responsible for the fully penetrant disease in Family I, which ranged from transient hypogammaglobulinemia and specific antibody deficiency to CVID.

Schubert et al. (2018) noted that the patients had no clinical symptoms other than infections. Serum levels of liver- and pancreas-secreted proteins were normal. Laboratory values that are altered in SEC61A1-associated ADTKD were also normal in these patients.
